evidence_loop.label: the advice that argued against the cure — a permission advisor removed after the host solved the problem
evidence_loop.summary: ADR-0038 shipped an advisor that read a machine's tool-use history and recommended a permission configuration to reduce prompts. Claude Code then gained `auto`, a permission MODE deciding per call, which met the goal at a layer the advisor could not reach and left the advice pointing the wrong way: on this machine it proposed `default_mode: acceptEdits` while the host config read `auto`, an EMPTY allow set, and 8 deny patterns including `Bash(cd *)`, `Bash(cat *)` and `Bash(git status *)`. Inversion, not staleness — caused by severity poisoning, where one dangerous instance drags a whole pattern to deny (`cat *` denied on 322 allow / 1 deny; `du *` on a single observation). The Codex half was quieter and worse: `parseCodexRollout` recognizes only `local_shell_call` and `function_call` named `shell`, and across 33,009 rollout lines the shapes present are `custom_tool_call:exec` (1,006) and `function_call:exec_command` (314). Recognized observations: 0. ADR-0057 removes the advisor and keeps the one permission fact runtime can still establish — that it relaxed nothing.

narrative:
This is the second consecutive loop to remove an overtaken layer — though only the first was still functioning when it went. The difference is where the answer came from: ADR-0056's matcher lost to arithmetic on a moving target; this advisor lost to the host shipping the cure.

ADR-0038's goal was fewer permission prompts, and its mechanism was advice: read the machine's tool-use history, grade each pattern, propose a configuration. Claude Code then added `auto` — a permission MODE deciding per call rather than a ruleset fixed in advance. That met the goal at a layer the advisor could not reach, and left the advice pointing the wrong way. The measurement is what makes this a removal rather than a rewrite: the advisor recommended `default_mode: acceptEdits` while the host's own config read `auto`, produced an EMPTY allow set, and named 8 deny patterns including `Bash(cd *)`, `Bash(cat *)` and `Bash(git status *)`. Applying that fragment would have made the session strictly worse.

The cause was traced, not assumed, and it is not a grading bug — `gradeCommand` in isolation is correct. It is severity poisoning: one dangerous instance drags an entire pattern to deny. `cat *` was denied on 322 allow against 1 deny; `git status *` on 16 against 1; `du *` on a single compound observation. Two of the eight deny patterns rest on one instance each. An earlier draft also credited `auto` with causing the empty allow set; that was wrong and is recorded as wrong — auto mode causes neither the deny set nor the empty allow set.

The Codex half is the part worth carrying forward, because it is a class rather than an instance. `parseCodexRollout` recognizes only `local_shell_call` and `function_call` named `shell`. Across this machine's 100 most recent rollouts — 33,009 JSONL lines — the shapes present are `custom_tool_call:exec` (1,006) and `function_call:exec_command` (314); `function_call:shell` never appears. Recognized observations: 0. The Codex advisor had been reading nothing, silently, for as long as that drift existed. A zero is a claim about the reader, not the world, and only an input-shape histogram against a control tells those apart.

That cuts both ways and the ADR states both. It removes the comfortable reading that Codex was fine, and it supplies the removal's argument in a new form: a capability whose Codex half produced zero observations, undetected, is one nobody relied on. But the regression is real and is not softened — Claude's operators lost an advisor and gained a better host mechanism; Codex's operators lost one and gained nothing, because Codex ships a rules-and-configuration engine (`execpolicy`, found 45 times in the real 228 MB binary with known-true control tokens behaving) and not a per-call decision mode. That was measured against the binary because the packaged baseline mentions `execpolicy` zero times, and silence is not evidence of absence.

What survives is the narrow, defensible fact: runtime relaxed nothing. `proof.permission` reads as advisor machinery because of its name and its old Stage-6 gate, and it is not. Its applicability was gated on an advisory fragment, so removing the advisor without rewriting that gate would have retired the assertion in silence. §Decision 5 decoupled it. This loop's proof shows the boundary proof still executes and passes; the rewrite itself is carried by source and tests, since a direct invocation bypasses the bootstrap applicability row.

One process reading belongs here because it repeated. This recovery's first byte-identity measurement was taken against `~/.codex/plugins/cache` — the exact mistake the scorecard already documents an earlier recovery making. The trees happened to agree, so the number did not change, but a written warning was walked into anyway, and the published value is the re-run one. The digest recipe got the same treatment: control-verified against the retained 0.96.0 cache first.
